Basons
BAY-sunz
noun
From Old French bacin, a wide vessel; the older English spelling of basins, rendering Hebrew mizrāq—the bowls of the altar that caught and cast the sacrificial blood.

Biblical Definition

Basons are the wide bowls of the sanctuary, and chief among their uses was the handling of blood: they caught the blood of the sacrifices and bore it to be sprinkled upon and about the altar. They are numbered among the brazen vessels, “his shovels, and his basons, and his fleshhooks” (Exo 27:3), and in the temple they were of gold (1Ch 28:17). At the sealing of the covenant at Sinai, “Moses took half of the blood, and put it in basons; and half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar” (Exo 24:6)—the very vessels that bound Israel to the LORD in blood. So the bason is the vessel of the blood, and the blood is the life, and the life poured out makes atonement (Lev 17:11). Every day the priests filled these bowls at the altar and cast the crimson against its sides, a ceaseless witness that without shedding of blood is no remission (Heb 9:22). All this pointed forward: the basons of brass and gold could only carry the blood of beasts, which cannot take away sin; but they preached the Blood that could. When Zechariah foretells the LORD’s people made mighty, they are “filled like bowls, and as the corners of the altar” (Zec 9:15)—filled as the blood-bowls of the sanctuary, dedicated wholly to God. The bason teaches that at the centre of true worship stands atoning blood.

Webster 1828 Definition

The wide altar-bowls that caught and cast the sacrificial blood—vessels that preach atonement at the heart of worship.

expand to see more

BASONS, wide, hollow vessels or bowls (the older spelling of basins).

Among the brazen vessels of the altar (Exo 27:3), and of gold in the temple (1Ch 28:17).

Their chief use was to receive and to sprinkle the blood of the sacrifices.

The vessels of the covenant-blood sprinkled at Sinai (Exo 24:6).

A figure of worship centred on atoning blood (Heb 9:22).

Key Scripture

Exo 27:3 — "And thou shalt make his pans to receive his ashes, and his shovels, and his basons, and his fleshhooks, and his firepans: all the vessels thereof thou shalt make of brass."

Exo 24:6 — "And Moses took half of the blood, and put it in basons; and half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar."

Num 7:13 — "And his offering was one silver charger, the weight thereof was an hundred and thirty shekels, one silver bowl of seventy shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary; both of them were full of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering:"

Zec 9:15 — "The LORD of hosts shall defend them; and they shall devour, and subdue with sling stones; and they shall drink, and make a noise as through wine; and they shall be filled like bowls, and as the corners of the altar."

Modern Corruption

A bowl of the altar, not a contested doctrine; the bason recovers the blood at the centre of worship, which the age would gladly forget.

expand to see more

The temptation the bason rebukes is the modern flight from blood—the wish for a worship swept clean of sacrifice, a gospel without an altar, a religion of sentiment that finds the crimson bowls of Scripture crude. But the God of the sanctuary set the blood-bason at the heart of His house and never took it thence, for without shedding of blood is no remission. To empty worship of atonement is to keep the temple and lose the reason for it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the centrality of atoning blood: the basons caught the life poured out (Lev 17:11), and all their sprinkling pointed to the Blood of Christ, which alone cleanseth from all sin (1Jn 1:7). True worship does not blush at the bason; it glories in the Lamb slain, and is filled like the bowls of the altar, wholly the LORD’s.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Wide altar-bowls, Hebrew mizrāq, that caught and sprinkled the sacrificial blood upon the altar.

expand to see more

Basons — Old French bacin; older English for basins; Hebrew mizrāq.

Brazen vessels of the altar (Exo 27:3); of gold in the temple (1Ch 28:17).

Their chief office was the receiving and sprinkling of blood.

The covenant-blood at Sinai was put in basons (Exo 24:6).

A figure of worship filled with, and founded on, atoning blood (Zec 9:15; Heb 9:22).

Usage

"At the centre of true worship stands atoning blood, caught in the bason and cast on the altar."

"To empty worship of sacrifice is to keep the temple and lose the reason for it."

"The people of the LORD are filled like the blood-bowls, wholly dedicated to Him."
